Why split. The supplied 15-step proof chains independent obligations of different kinds:
- linear algebra: orthonormal coordinates adapted to the orientation (steps 1–3);
- the inverse function theorem with a C¹ inverse (step 6);
- the local graph representation of an embedded C² submanifold through a proper chart (steps 4–8);
- a purely metric cylinder argument (steps 9–10);
- a connectedness argument fixing the sign of the orientation along the graph (steps 11–15).
A leaf proof must be one appended declaration with no helper lemma and no set_option (leaf_verification.check_source_delta), so the unsplit proof would be a single tactic block of about 450 lines. Each new child is a reusable lemma: the C¹ inverse function theorem on an open target; an embedded submanifold is locally a graph over a plane containing its tangent space; the cylinder reformulation; and the orientation along a graph through x is the normalized Jacobian orientation.

- local_inverse (codim1_zsl_gc_local_inverse): step 6, the inverse function theorem for any C¹ map φ : ℝ^d → ℝ^d with injective Dφ(z₀).

How the children prove the selected theorem (checked in Lean).
1. IsOrientation at x gives Q₀ with (Q₀ : Set) = tangentSpace N x and IsUnitOrientationOf (ξN x) Q₀.
2. oriented_frame n k Q₀ (ξN x) gives ι, ι' with (a), Set.range ι = Q₀ and (d). Hence tangentSpace N x ⊆ Set.range ι.
3. local_graph (n + 1) k N x ι ι' gives O, u, s.
4. u is C¹ on the open set O ∋ 0, so u is continuous at 0. graph_cylinder (n + 1) k N x ι ι' O u s then gives δ₁, δ₂ with ball 0 δ₁ ⊆ O, u(B_{δ₁}) ⊆ B_{δ₂} and (c).
5. ContDiffOn ℝ 1 u (ball 0 δ₁) follows by monotonicity. With u 0 = 0 and fderiv ℝ u 0 = 0 from local_graph, this gives (b).
6. orientation_along_graph n k N ξN x ι ι' u δ₁ gives (e). Its hypotheses are IsOrientation, orthogonality, δ₁ > 0, C¹ on the ball, u 0 = 0, Du(0) = 0, Γ(B_{δ₁}) ⊆ N (from local_graph and ball 0 δ₁ ⊆ O) and (d).

subproblems.title: Orthonormal coordinates adapted to a unit (n+1)-orientation of a plane (parent steps 1–3)
subproblems.statement: Let n, k ∈ ℕ, P := n + 1 + k, let Q ⊆ ℝ^P be a linear subspace and let ξ ∈ Λ_{n+1}(ℝ^P) (MultiVector P (n+1): continuous linear functionals on (n+1)-covectors) be a unit orientation of Q (IsUnitOrientationOf ξ Q: there is an orthonormal family τ : Fin (n+1) → ℝ^P with span(range τ) = Q such that ξ(α) = α(τ) for all α, or ξ(α) = −α(τ) for all α). Then there are linear isometries ι : ℝ^{n+1} → ℝ^P and ι' : ℝ^k → ℝ^P such that ⟨ιv, ι'w⟩ = 0 for all v ∈ ℝ^{n+1}, w ∈ ℝ^k; every y ∈ ℝ^P equals ιv + ι'w for some v, w; range ι = Q (as sets); and ξ(α) = α(ιe_0, …, ιe_n) for every (n+1)-covector α, where e_j = EuclideanSpace.single j 1 is the standard basis of ℝ^{n+1}.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n k : ℕ) (Q : Submodule ℝ (Euclid (n + 1 + k))) (ξ : MultiVector (n + 1 + k) (n + 1)), IsUnitOrientationOf ξ Q → ∃ (ι : Euclid (n + 1) →ₗᵢ[ℝ] Euclid (n + 1 + k)) (ι' : Euclid k →ₗᵢ[ℝ] Euclid (n + 1 + k)), (∀ v w, inner ℝ (ι v) (ι' w) = 0) ∧ (∀ y : Euclid (n + 1 + k), ∃ v w, y = ι v + ι' w) ∧ Set.range ι = (Q : Set (Euclid (n + 1 + k))) ∧ ∀ α : Covector (Euclid (n + 1 + k)) (n + 1), ξ α = α (fun j => ι (EuclideanSpace.single j (1 : ℝ)))
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source. Steps 1–3 of the supplied proof of the selected node graph_chart (Submission.codim1_zsl_oriented_graph_chart), with Q₀ := Q and ξ_N(x) := ξ. Orientations: Simon Ch. 6, 1.1 and 2.2. Uses the accepted declarations Submission.dorag_lip_orthonormal_coordinates (sibling key orthonormal_coordinates; it is parent step 2) and Submission.rsdic_unitOrientation_eq_or_eq_neg (sibling key orientation_sign).
Notation. P := n + 1 + k; e_j := EuclideanSpace.single j 1 ∈ ℝ^{n+1} (j ∈ Fin (n+1)), the standard orthonormal basis; for a family c : Fin (n+1) → ℝ^P and an (n+1)-covector α (a continuous alternating (n+1)-linear map ℝ^P → ℝ), α(c) is the value of α on c.
1. (dim Q = n + 1; parent step 1.) By hypothesis there is an orthonormal family τ : Fin (n+1) → ℝ^P with span(range τ) = Q (and a sign, not needed here). An orthonormal family is linearly independent (Orthonormal.linearIndependent), so finrank Q = finrank span(range τ) = card(Fin (n+1)) = n + 1 (finrank_span_eq_card, Fintype.card_fin).
2. (Orthonormal coordinates; parent step 2.) Apply Submission.dorag_lip_orthonormal_coordinates with n + 1 in place of n, the same k, and T₀ := Q; its hypothesis finrank Q = n + 1 is step 1, and Euclid ((n+1) + k) is literally Euclid (n + 1 + k). It gives linear isometries ι₀ : ℝ^{n+1} → ℝ^P and ι' : ℝ^k → ℝ^P with (a) ⟨ι₀v, ι'w⟩ = 0 for all v, w; (b) ι₀v ∈ Q for all v; (c) every y ∈ ℝ^P equals ι₀v + ι'w for some v, w; (d) p_Q(ι₀v + ι'w) = ι₀v for all v, w, where p_Q = Q.starProjection is the orthogonal projection onto Q.
3. (range ι₀ = Q.) The inclusion range ι₀ ⊆ Q is (b). Conversely, let q ∈ Q and write q = ι₀v + ι'w by (c). Since q ∈ Q, p_Q q = q (Submodule.starProjection_eq_self_iff), while p_Q q = ι₀v by (d). Hence q = ι₀v ∈ range ι₀.
4. (The orientation ζ₀ of the frame ι₀e; parent step 3.) Let τ₀ := (ι₀e_0, …, ι₀e_n). It is orthonormal, being the image of the orthonormal family (e_j) (EuclideanSpace.orthonormal_single) under the linear isometry ι₀ (Orthonormal.comp_linearIsometry). Its span is contained in Q by (b), and it has dimension n + 1 because τ₀ is linearly independent (finrank_span_eq_card); as finrank Q = n + 1 (step 1), span(range τ₀) = Q (Submodule.eq_of_le_of_finrank_eq). Let ζ₀ ∈ MultiVector P (n+1) be evaluation at τ₀, ζ₀(α) := α(τ₀): this is the continuous linear map ContinuousAlternatingMap.apply ℝ (Euclid P) ℝ τ₀, and ζ₀(α) = α(τ₀) holds by definition. Thus IsUnitOrientationOf ζ₀ Q, witnessed by τ₀ with the + sign.
5. (Sign.) ζ₀ and ξ are unit orientations of the same subspace Q, so Submission.rsdic_unitOrientation_eq_or_eq_neg (with v := ζ₀, w := ξ) gives ξ = ζ₀ or ξ = −ζ₀.
6. (Case ξ = ζ₀.) Take ι := ι₀ and ι' from step 2. Orthogonality is (a), the decomposition is (c), range ι = Q is step 3, and ξ(α) = ζ₀(α) = α(ι₀e_0, …, ι₀e_n) for every α.
7. (Case ξ = −ζ₀.) Let K := (span{e_0})^⊥ ⊆ ℝ^{n+1} and let ρ := K.reflection, the reflection in the hyperplane K, a linear isometric equivalence of ℝ^{n+1}. Then ρ(e_0) = −e_0 (Submodule.reflection_orthogonalComplement_singleton_eq_neg); for j ≠ 0, ⟨e_0, e_j⟩ = 0, i.e. e_j ∈ K (Submodule.mem_orthogonal_singleton_iff_inner_right, EuclideanSpace.inner_single_left), so ρ(e_j) = e_j (Submodule.reflection_mem_subspace_eq_self); and ρ(ρ(v)) = v for all v (Submodule.reflection_reflection). Put ι := ι₀ ∘ ρ (a linear isometry, ι₀.comp ρ.toLinearIsometry) and keep ι'.
 (i) ⟨ιv, ι'w⟩ = ⟨ι₀(ρv), ι'w⟩ = 0 by (a).
 (ii) Given y ∈ ℝ^P, write y = ι₀v + ι'w by (c); then y = ι(ρv) + ι'w because ι(ρv) = ι₀(ρ(ρv)) = ι₀v.
 (iii) range ι = range ι₀ = Q, because ρ is surjective (Function.Surjective.range_comp) and by step 3.
 (iv) The family (ιe_0, …, ιe_n) is τ₀ with its 0-th entry replaced by (−1)·ι₀e_0, i.e. Function.update τ₀ 0 ((−1)·τ₀ 0): indeed ιe_0 = ι₀(−e_0) = −ι₀e_0 and ιe_j = ι₀e_j for j ≠ 0. By linearity of α in the 0-th slot (ContinuousAlternatingMap.map_update_smul, then Function.update_eq_self), α(ιe_0, …, ιe_n) = (−1)·α(τ₀) = −ζ₀(α) = ξ(α) for every α.
 Hence ι, ι' satisfy all four conclusions.
8. In both cases the required ι and ι' exist. ∎

Then there are an open set O ⊆ ℝ^d with 0 ∈ O, a map u : ℝ^d → ℝ^k and s > 0 such that u is C¹ on O, u(0) = 0, Du(0) = 0 (fderiv ℝ u 0 = 0), x + ιv + ι'u(v) ∈ N for every v ∈ O, and every y ∈ N with |y − x| < s equals x + ιv + ι'u(v) for some v ∈ O.

Hence τ and τ' are orthonormal bases b and b' of Q indexed by Fin n.

3. Let d := det_b(b'), the determinant of the change-of-basis matrix from b to b'. Both bases are orthonormal, so this matrix is orthogonal and d ∈ {1, −1} (Mathlib OrthonormalBasis.det_to_matrix_orthonormalBasis_real).

 (b) By the quotient rule, h'(t) = ((1 + t²/c²) − t·(2t/c²))/(1 + t²/c²)² = (1 − t²/c²)/(1 + t²/c²)². So h'(0) = 1.
 (c) |h(t)| ≤ c/2 for every t ∈ ℝ. Indeed |h(t)| = |t|/(1 + t²/c²) = c²|t|/(c² + t²). Also c² + t² − 2c|t| = (c − |t|)² ≥ 0, which gives c²|t| ≤ (c/2)(c² + t²).
3. Let β(t) := v + h(t)a for t ∈ ℝ. By 2(c), |β(t) − v| = |h(t)||a| ≤ (c/2)|a| = ρ₀/2 < ρ₀. So β(t) ∈ ball(v, ρ₀) ⊆ V for every t ∈ ℝ. By 2(a), β is C¹ on ℝ and β(0) = v + 0·a = v. By 2(b), β has derivative h'(0)a = a at t = 0.

Source: Simon Ch. 2, §4, Definition (4.1) and the remark before (4.2) (book/chapter-02.txt, lines 849–862). There Simon notes that "the above definition ensures the local representation is a homeomorphism of V onto the image M ∩ W"; the properness condition of (4.1) is what makes this work. Fix v ∈ V and ε > 0, and write q := ψ(v).
1. Suppose, for a contradiction, that no δ > 0 has the stated property. Then for every j ∈ ℕ the number δ = 1/(j+1) > 0 fails. So there is v_j ∈ V with |ψ(v_j) − q| < 1/(j+1) and |v_j − v| ≥ ε.
2. We have 0 ≤ |ψ(v_j) − q| < 1/(j+1) and 1/(j+1) → 0. By squeezing, ψ(v_j) → q as j → ∞.
3. Let K := {q} ∪ {ψ(v_j) : j ∈ ℕ}. K is compact because it is the range of a convergent sequence together with its limit. Indeed, given an open cover of K, one member contains q, and by step 2 it contains ψ(v_j) for all j ≥ j₀. Finitely many further members cover ψ(v_0), …, ψ(v_{j₀−1}).
4. K ⊆ W. For each j, v_j ∈ V, so ψ(v_j) ∈ ψ(V) ⊆ W. Also v ∈ V, so q = ψ(v) ∈ ψ(V) ⊆ W.
5. By the properness hypothesis applied to the compact set K ⊆ W, the set C := V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) is compact. Every v_j lies in C, because v_j ∈ V and ψ(v_j) ∈ K. C is a compact subset of the metric space ℝ^d, hence sequentially compact. So there are a strictly increasing φ : ℕ → ℕ and a point v* ∈ C with v_{φ(i)} → v* as i → ∞. In particular v* ∈ V.
6. Now v* ∈ V, every v_{φ(i)} lies in V, and v_{φ(i)} → v*. Since ψ is continuous on V, it is continuous at v* relative to V, so ψ(v_{φ(i)}) → ψ(v*). On the other hand, (ψ(v_{φ(i)}))_i is a subsequence of (ψ(v_j))_j, so ψ(v_{φ(i)}) → q by step 2. Limits in ℝ^P are unique, hence ψ(v*) = q = ψ(v).
7. Both v* and v lie in V, and ψ is injective on V, so v* = v. Thus v_{φ(i)} → v. Hence |v_{φ(i)} − v| < ε for some i. This contradicts step 1, which gives |v_j − v| ≥ ε for every j, in particular for j = φ(i).
8. So the assumption in step 1 is false. There is δ > 0 such that every v' ∈ V with |ψ(v') − ψ(v)| < δ satisfies |v' − v| < ε. Since v ∈ V and ε > 0 were arbitrary, the statement is proved.
proof_key_steps: Negating the claim gives v_j ∈ V with |ψ(v_j) − ψ(v)| < 1/(j+1) and |v_j − v| ≥ ε, so ψ(v_j) → ψ(v).
K = {ψ(v)} ∪ {ψ(v_j)} is compact and lies in W, so V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) is compact and contains every v_j.
A subsequence v_{φ(i)} converges to some v* ∈ V. Continuity of ψ on V and uniqueness of limits give ψ(v*) = ψ(v).
Injectivity on V gives v* = v, which contradicts |v_{φ(i)} − v| ≥ ε.
